questions.question: What is backtracking and how does it differ from regular recursion?
questions.title: Backtracking Introduction Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Backtracking** is recursion that **builds a candidate step by step and undoes (backtracks) a choice when it can't lead to a valid solution**. The extra ingredients over plain recursion are **choose -> explore -> un-choose** and **pruning** (abandoning dead branches early). It explores the **decision tree** of all possibilities, making it ideal for permutations, subsets, N-Queens, and constraint problems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can articulate the choose/explore/unchoose loop and pruning, versus generic recursion
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating backtracking as 'just recursion', or forgetting to undo the choice after exploring
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Emphasize the un-choose (state restoration) step and pruning as what makes it backtracking

sections.title: Backtracking vs Plain Recursion
sections.content:
All backtracking is recursion, but not all recursion is backtracking. **Plain recursion** breaks a problem into subproblems and combines results (e.g. factorial, Fibonacci). **Backtracking** incrementally **builds a candidate solution**, and the moment a partial candidate **can't possibly lead to a valid full solution**, it **abandons it and undoes the last choice**.

The defining loop is **choose -> explore -> un-choose**: make a choice, recurse to extend it, then **restore the state** so you can try the next option. Two things distinguish it: that **un-choose (state restoration)** step, and **pruning** - cutting off dead branches early to avoid exploring the entire search space. It's the go-to for **permutations, subsets, combinations, N-Queens, Sudoku, and word search**.

sections.title: Backtracking at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Plain recursion|~split and combine|factorial, Fibonacci|returns a value|no state to undo
emerald|Backtracking|~build incrementally|choose, explore, un-choose|tries all options|restores state
amber|Pruning|~cut dead branches|stop early if invalid|skip impossible paths|huge speedup
rose|Use cases|~explore decision tree|permutations, subsets|N-Queens, Sudoku|word search, combos

sections.title: The Backtracking Template
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting to un-choose**: not restoring state after the recursive call corrupts later branches.
- **No pruning**: exploring obviously-invalid branches blows up the runtime.
- **Adding by reference**: store a **copy** (snapshot) of the solution, not the mutable working list.
- **Calling it plain recursion**: the undo + pruning are the distinguishing features.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Backtracking = recursion + **choose/explore/un-choose** + **pruning**.
- The **un-choose** (state restoration) step is essential.
- **Pruning** abandons dead branches early.
- Explores the **decision tree** of all candidates.
- Used for permutations, subsets, N-Queens, Sudoku, word search.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: All backtracking is recursion, but not all recursion is backtracking, and the difference is what makes this question interesting. Plain recursion typically breaks a problem into subproblems, solves them, and combines the results, like computing factorial or Fibonacci. Backtracking is a specific style of recursion where I build up a candidate solution one choice at a time, and the key idea is that the moment a partial candidate can't possibly lead to a valid complete solution, I abandon it and undo my last choice. The defining pattern is choose, explore, un-choose. I make a choice, I recurse to explore where that choice leads, and then critically I undo the choice, restoring the state so I can try the next option from the same point. That undo step, restoring state after exploring, is the single thing that most distinguishes backtracking from plain recursion, and it's also the thing freshers most often forget, which corrupts the results for the sibling branches. The other distinguishing feature is pruning: before I even explore a branch, I check whether it can lead anywhere valid, and if not, I skip it entirely. Pruning is what keeps backtracking from blindly exploring an exponential search space. Conceptually, I'm walking a decision tree of all possible candidates, going deep, and retreating whenever I hit a dead end. This is the pattern behind permutations, subsets, combinations, N-Queens, Sudoku solvers, and word search. One last tip: when I record a solution, I store a copy of it, not the mutable working list, otherwise later undo operations will mutate what I already saved.

groups.heading: Regular recursion
groups.text: A function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Each call is independent — it doesn't mutate shared state and doesn't need to clean up after itself. Factorial and Fibonacci are classic examples.

groups.heading: Backtracking
groups.text: A recursive technique that also mutates a shared state — the 'current path' — and then undoes that mutation after each recursive call returns. The three steps are: choose, explore, unchoose. Missing the unchoose step corrupts the state for every sibling branch.

items: Use regular recursion when you need one computed result and there's no state to track across branches.
Use backtracking when the problem says 'find all' or 'list all valid arrangements' and each branch modifies shared state.

beats.text: candidates miss: In N-Queens, every row's queen placement is added to a set before recursing and removed after — without that removal, the next column sees a 'full' board and skips valid placements entirely.

speakable_v2.cap: Backtracking equals recursion plus undo — if you don't restore state after each branch, your results are wrong.

questions.question: How do you generate all subsets of a set using backtracking?
questions.title: Generate All Subsets Backtracking Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Generate all **2^n subsets** with backtracking: at each index you make a binary choice - **include** the current element or **skip** it - then recurse to the next index. Add a copy of the current subset at every node (or only at the leaves). It's **O(2^n)** subsets, each up to length n, so **O(n * 2^n)** total work. The choose/recurse/un-choose pattern drives it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you model subsets as include/exclude decisions and remember to copy before adding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding the mutable list reference (all entries end up identical), or missing the un-choose step
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note there are 2^n subsets (binary choice per element) and you must snapshot the list

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **2^n** subsets: each element is **in or out**.
- Pattern: record copy -> for each later element **choose/recurse/un-choose**.
- Always **snapshot** the working list before adding.
- Recurse with `i + 1` to avoid reusing/duplicating.
- **O(n * 2^n)** total work.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The number of subsets of n elements is two to the n, and the reason is that each element is independently either included in a subset or not, that's a binary choice per element. That structure maps perfectly onto backtracking. I write a recursive helper that takes a start index and the current subset I'm building. At the top of each call, I record the current subset, which is how I capture subsets of every size, not just the full-length ones. Then I loop over the remaining elements from the start index onward, and for each one I do the classic three steps: I add the element to my current list, that's the choose step; I recurse with the next index to explore everything that follows; and then I remove the element I just added, that's the un-choose step, which restores the state so I can try the next element cleanly. The single most important implementation detail is that when I record a subset, I must add a copy of the current list, a new ArrayList, not the list reference itself. If I add the reference, then as the recursion continues to mutate that same list, every subset I stored will end up pointing to the same final state, which is the classic bug. The other detail is recursing with i plus one rather than start plus one, so I don't reuse the same element or generate duplicate subsets. The total work is O of n times two to the n, since there are two to the n subsets and copying each one costs up to n. If the input can have duplicates, I'd sort first and skip over equal elements at the same recursion level.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Use backtracking: at each step **try each candidate from a `start` index**, subtract it from the remaining target, and recurse.

If the remaining target hits **0**, record the combination; if it goes **negative**, **prune** that branch.

To allow **reusing** a number, recurse with the **same index**; to use each once, recurse with `i + 1`. Sorting enables an early break when `candidate > remaining`.

Treating backtracking as 'just recursion', or forgetting to undo the choice after exploring

sections.title: Subset Decision Tree
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[start, current=empty] --> B[record copy of current]
    B --> C{for i from start..n}
    C --> D[add nums i  CHOOSE]
    D --> E[recurse with i+1]
    E --> F[remove nums i  UN-CHOOSE]
    F --> C
    C -- done --> Z[all subsets recorded]
```

sections.title: Generate Subsets with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding the reference**: `res.add(cur)` stores the live list - all entries become identical at the end. Add a copy.
- **Forgetting un-choose**: not removing the last element after recursion corrupts sibling branches.
- **Wrong start index**: recurse with `i + 1` (not `start + 1`) to avoid duplicate subsets.
- **Duplicates in input**: sort and skip equal elements if the set may contain duplicates.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Use **backtracking** when you must **enumerate or construct all valid solutions** (permutations, subsets, N-Queens, Sudoku) - it explores the whole decision tree with pruning. Use **dynamic programming** when you need an **optimal value or a count** and the problem has **overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure** (knapsack, LCS, coin change). Backtracking is often **exponential**; DP reuses subproblem answers for **polynomial** time.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app solving a two-sum problem using a HashMap for O(n) lookup
speakable_v2.hook: Every element faces one question - in or out - and those n yes/no choices fan out into exactly 2^n subsets.

beats.text: Generating all subsets means finding every possible selection of elements from a set, including the empty selection and the full set itself. For n elements there are exactly 2^n subsets because each element has two states — included or excluded.

Many problems — combination sum, power set, feature selection — require exploring every possible subset. Backtracking lets us do this systematically by making one include/exclude decision per element rather than trying all combinations blindly.

items: Include/exclude approach: at each index branch into two recursive calls — one that adds the element, one that skips it. Record the current list at every call level, not just the leaves.
Loop-based approach: loop from a start index, add the element, recurse with start+1, then remove the element. Naturally extends to combination-sum by changing the start index behavior.

beats.text: non-obvious: For nums = [1, 2], the include/exclude tree has four leaves: [], [2], [1], [1,2]. But with the loop approach you collect results at every recursive call entry — [], [1], [1,2], [2] — same four subsets in a different traversal order. Both are correct; the loop approach extends more cleanly to combination problems.

items: Only collecting subsets at leaf nodes misses all intermediate subsets — you'd only get subsets of size n.
Not copying the list before adding to results means all entries point to the same mutable list — they'll all show the last state.

speakable_v2.cap: Collect results at every call level, not just leaves — and always copy the list before saving it.

questions.question: How do you find all combinations that sum to a target?
questions.title: Combination Sum Backtracking Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use backtracking: at each step **try each candidate from a `start` index**, subtract it from the remaining target, and recurse. If the remaining target hits **0**, record the combination; if it goes **negative**, **prune** that branch. To allow **reusing** a number, recurse with the **same index**; to use each once, recurse with `i + 1`. Sorting enables an early break when `candidate > remaining`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can structure the recursion with a start index and prune on negative/zero remaining
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Generating duplicate combinations (not using a start index) or forgetting the prune when target goes negative
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Control reuse via same-index vs i+1 recursion and add the sorted early-break pruning

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Track **remaining target**; record when it hits **0**, prune when **< 0**.
- Use a **`start` index** to avoid duplicate combinations.
- Recurse with **`i`** to reuse a number, **`i + 1`** to use it once.
- **Sort + break** when `candidate > remaining` for strong pruning.
- Store a **copy** of the path on success.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: I solve combination sum with backtracking, tracking how much target I have remaining. The recursive helper takes the remaining target, a start index, and the current path I'm building. There are two base cases. If the remaining target is exactly zero, I've found a valid combination, so I record a copy of the path. If the remaining target goes negative, this branch can't work, so I prune it and return immediately, that pruning is essential to keep the search efficient. Otherwise, I loop over the candidates starting from the start index, and for each one I subtract it from the remaining target and recurse. Using a start index, rather than always starting from zero, is what prevents me from generating duplicate combinations like two-three and three-two; I only ever move forward through the candidates. The reuse behavior is a one-line decision. If a number can be used multiple times, which is the classic combination sum, I recurse with the same index i. If each number can be used at most once, I recurse with i plus one. After the recursive call, I do the un-choose step, removing the element I added so I can try the next candidate. One nice optimization: if I sort the candidates first, then inside the loop, the moment a candidate is larger than the remaining target I can break out entirely, because every later candidate is even bigger and also can't fit. And as always, when I record a successful combination I add a copy of the path, not the live list.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Use backtracking: at each step **try each candidate from a `start` index**, subtract it from the remaining target, and recurse.

If the remaining target hits **0**, record the combination; if it goes **negative**, **prune** that branch.

To allow **reusing** a number, recurse with the **same index**; to use each once, recurse with `i + 1`. Sorting enables an early break when `candidate > remaining`.

Treating backtracking as 'just recursion', or forgetting to undo the choice after exploring

sections.title: Combination Sum Recursion
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[remaining = target
start = 0] --> B{remaining == 0?} B -- yes --> S[record copy of path] B -- no --> C{remaining < 0?} C -- yes --> P[prune: return] C -- no --> D{for i from start..n} D --> E[choose nums i
remaining -= nums i] E --> F[recurse same i = reuse] F --> G[un-choose: add back] G --> D ```

sections.title: Combination Sum with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No start index**: iterating from 0 each time produces duplicate combinations like [2,3] and [3,2].
- **Missing prune**: not returning when remaining < 0 wastes huge amounts of work.
- **Wrong reuse**: recurse with `i` to reuse, `i + 1` for single-use - pick deliberately.
- **Adding the reference**: store a copy of `path` on success.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Use **backtracking** when you must **enumerate or construct all valid solutions** (permutations, subsets, N-Queens, Sudoku) - it explores the whole decision tree with pruning. Use **dynamic programming** when you need an **optimal value or a count** and the problem has **overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure** (knapsack, LCS, coin change). Backtracking is often **exponential**; DP reuses subproblem answers for **polynomial** time.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app solving a two-sum problem using a HashMap for O(n) lookup
speakable_v2.hook: Subtract as you go, and the search prunes itself - the instant the remaining target drops below zero, that whole branch is dead.

beats.text: Combination sum asks for all unique combinations of candidates that add up to a target value. Candidates may be reused (unbounded) or used once each. You need to enumerate every valid combination, not just count them.

Brute force tries every possible multiset, which explodes combinatorially. Backtracking explores only promising paths by tracking a running sum and cutting off branches the moment they exceed the target — that's pruning.

items: Sort candidates first so that once a candidate exceeds the remaining target you can break the loop — every element to the right is larger.
Recurse with the same index i when reuse is allowed, or i+1 when each candidate can be used only once.

beats.text: sharp edge: Candidates [2, 3, 6, 7], target 7. After sorting, when i=2 (value 6) and remaining is 1, break immediately rather than continuing to 7 — saves the entire 7-subtree. Without the sort + break, the loop visits every candidate for every remaining value.

items: Skipping the pruning break means the recursion still finds correct results but runs far longer than needed — expect TLE on large inputs.
Forgetting to copy the list before adding to results gives all result entries the same mutable reference — they'll all reflect the final empty state.

speakable_v2.cap: Sort, prune with a break, and copy the list on success — those three habits keep combination sum both correct and fast.

questions.question: How do you solve the N-Queens problem?
questions.title: N-Queens Backtracking Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Place queens **one row at a time**. For each row, try each column; a column is valid if no queen shares its **column or either diagonal**. If valid, place the queen and recurse to the next row; on return, **remove it (backtrack)**. Track attacked columns and diagonals with **boolean sets** for O(1) checks. Diagonals are identified by `row - col` and `row + col`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you structure it row-by-row and check column + both diagonals efficiently
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Checking only columns (missing diagonals), or doing O(n) scans per placement instead of O(1) sets
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use row-col and row+col to index diagonals and place one queen per row to cut the search space

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Place **one queen per row** -> only choose a column.
- Conflicts: same **column**, `r-c` diagonal, `r+c` diagonal.
- Use **boolean sets** for **O(1)** validity checks.
- Offset `r - c` by `n` to keep array indices non-negative.
- choose -> recurse -> **un-choose** the flags.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: N-Queens is the canonical backtracking problem. I have to place n queens on an n by n board so that no two attack each other, meaning no two share a row, a column, or a diagonal. The first simplification, which is really important, is that I place exactly one queen per row. That immediately removes all row conflicts and means that for each row I only have to choose a column, which dramatically cuts the search space. So I go row by row. For the current row, I try each column, and a column is safe if no previously placed queen is in that same column or on either of the two diagonals through that square. The clever part is identifying the diagonals cheaply. For one diagonal family, the value row minus column is constant along it, and for the other family, row plus column is constant. So I keep three boolean arrays: one for columns, one for the row-minus-column diagonals, and one for the row-plus-column diagonals. That lets me check whether a square is under attack in O of one instead of scanning the whole board each time. When I find a safe column, I mark all three flags, that's the choose step, recurse to the next row to explore, and then when the recursion returns I clear those flags, the un-choose step. When I successfully place a queen in every row, I've found a valid arrangement. One small implementation detail: row minus column can be negative, so I offset it by n when indexing the array. Checking only columns and forgetting the diagonals is the classic mistake here.

sections.title: Reason through the problem
sections.content:
Use backtracking: at each step **try each candidate from a `start` index**, subtract it from the remaining target, and recurse.

If the remaining target hits **0**, record the combination; if it goes **negative**, **prune** that branch.

Place queens **one row at a time**. For each row, try each column; a column is valid if no queen shares its **column or either diagonal**. If valid, place the queen and recurse to the next row; on return, **remove it (backtrack)**. Track attacked columns and diagonals with **boolean sets** for O(1) checks. Diagonals are identified by `row - col` and `row + col`.

Treating backtracking as 'just recursion', or forgetting to undo the choice after exploring

sections.title: N-Queens Row-by-Row
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[solve row r] --> B{r == n?} B -- yes --> S[record solution] B -- no --> C{for col c in 0..n} C --> D{col, r-c, r+c
all free?} D -- no --> C D -- yes --> E[place queen
mark sets] E --> F[recurse row r+1] F --> G[remove queen
unmark sets] G --> C ```

sections.title: N-Queens with O(1) Conflict Checks
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only checking columns**: you must also block both **diagonals** (`r-c`, `r+c`).
- **O(n) safety scan**: scanning the board each placement is slow; use boolean sets for O(1).
- **Negative diagonal index**: `r - c` can be negative - offset by `n` for array indexing.
- **Forgetting to un-mark**: clear the column/diagonal flags after recursion.

sections.content: Use **backtracking** when you must **enumerate or construct all valid solutions** (permutations, subsets, N-Queens, Sudoku) - it explores the whole decision tree with pruning. Use **dynamic programming** when you need an **optimal value or a count** and the problem has **overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure** (knapsack, LCS, coin change). Backtracking is often **exponential**; DP reuses subproblem answers for **polynomial** time.

seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for How do you solve the N-Queens problem? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app solving a two-sum problem using a HashMap for O(n) lookup
speakable_v2.hook: The trick that tames N-Queens: one queen per row, and two subtractions - row minus col, row plus col - to spot every diagonal in O(1).

beats.text: N-Queens asks you to place N queens on an N×N chessboard so no two queens threaten each other — no shared row, column, or diagonal. Because one queen per row is forced, you only decide which column to use in each row.
Trying every board configuration is N^(N*N) states — impossible. Placing row-by-row with immediate conflict pruning collapses the search space dramatically, making even N=8 (92 solutions) fast.

items: Column conflict: track used columns in a Set — O(1) lookup.
Left diagonal conflict: row − col is the same for all cells on the same left diagonal.
Right diagonal conflict: row + col is the same for all cells on the same right diagonal.

beats.text: candidates miss: The diagonal check is row − col and row + col, not absolute differences. Using Math.abs(rowDiff) == Math.abs(colDiff) works but requires O(n) iteration over previous queens — three Sets give O(1). For N=4, the first valid solution is columns [1,3,0,2].

items: Forgetting to remove from all three sets on backtrack leaves stale conflict data that blocks valid future placements.
Only checking column conflicts and missing diagonals gives too many 'solutions' that aren't actually valid.

speakable_v2.cap: Three sets — columns, left diagonals, right diagonals — give O(1) conflict checks; always remove from all three on backtrack.

questions.question: How do you generate all permutations of an array using backtracking?
questions.title: Generate All Permutations Using Backtracking
questions.direct_answer: Build each permutation by **picking an unused element at every position** and recursing. Track used elements with a **boolean[] used** (or swap in place). When the path length equals `n`, record a copy. There are **n!** permutations, each length n, so **O(n * n!)** total. The choose/recurse/un-choose pattern with a `used` marker prevents reusing an element within one permutation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you avoid reusing elements via a used[] flag (or swap) and snapshot on completion
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reusing the same element in a permutation, or adding the mutable list reference
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the in-place swap variant and handling duplicates by sorting + skipping

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **n!** permutations; build one position at a time.
- Use **`used[]`** (or in-place swaps) to avoid reusing elements.
- Record a **copy** when path length == n.
- **O(n * n!)** total work.
- Handle duplicates with **sort + skip**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A permutation is an arrangement that uses every element exactly once, and there are n factorial of them. I generate them all with backtracking, building one permutation position by position. At each position, I try placing every element that hasn't already been used in the current permutation. To track that, I keep a boolean used array, where used at index i tells me whether the i-th element is already in my current path. So in the loop, if an element is used, I skip it; otherwise I mark it used and add it to the path, that's the choose step, recurse to fill the next position, and then when the recursion returns I unmark it and remove it from the path, the un-choose step. When my path reaches length n, I've built a complete permutation, so I record a copy of it. The total work is O of n times n factorial, since there are n factorial permutations and copying each one costs n. There's also an alternative in-place swap approach, where instead of a used array I swap the current index with each of the later indices, which generates permutations by rearranging the array itself; it saves the extra array but mutates the input. The two mistakes to avoid are reusing an element within a single permutation, which the used array prevents, and adding the live path list instead of a copy when recording a result. If the input contains duplicate values and I want only distinct permutations, I sort the array first and skip an element when it equals the previous element and that previous element hasn't been used at this level, which avoids generating duplicate arrangements.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Use backtracking: at each step **try each candidate from a `start` index**, subtract it from the remaining target, and recurse.

If the remaining target hits **0**, record the combination; if it goes **negative**, **prune** that branch.

To allow **reusing** a number, recurse with the **same index**; to use each once, recurse with `i + 1`. Sorting enables an early break when `candidate > remaining`.

Treating backtracking as 'just recursion', or forgetting to undo the choice after exploring

sections.title: Permutation Build
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[path empty
used all false] --> B{path.size == n?} B -- yes --> S[record copy] B -- no --> C{for i in 0..n} C --> D{used i ?} D -- yes --> C D -- no --> E[add nums i
used i = true] E --> F[recurse] F --> G[remove last
used i = false] G --> C ```

sections.title: Permutations with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reusing an element**: without `used[]` (or swapping), you get invalid repeats like [1,1,2].
- **Adding the reference**: snapshot the path on completion, don't add the live list.
- **Forgetting to reset `used[i]`**: must clear it during un-choose.
- **Duplicates producing repeats**: sort and skip `nums[i] == nums[i-1] && !used[i-1]`.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Use **backtracking** when you must **enumerate or construct all valid solutions** (permutations, subsets, N-Queens, Sudoku) - it explores the whole decision tree with pruning. Use **dynamic programming** when you need an **optimal value or a count** and the problem has **overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure** (knapsack, LCS, coin change). Backtracking is often **exponential**; DP reuses subproblem answers for **polynomial** time.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app solving a two-sum problem using a HashMap for O(n) lookup
speakable_v2.hook: Each slot grabs an unused element and the rest recurse - flip a single 'used' flag and n! orderings unfold.

beats.text: Generating all permutations means producing every possible ordering of n elements. For n elements there are n! orderings. The in-place swap approach does this without an extra visited array.

The swap-based approach avoids allocating a separate 'used' boolean array. By swapping elements into the current position and swapping back after recursion, we naturally rotate all candidates through each index.

items: Choose: swap arr[start] with arr[j] to place candidate j at the current position.
Explore: recurse with start+1 to fill the remainder.
Unchoose: swap arr[start] back with arr[j] to restore the array for the next iteration.

beats.text: production trap: Missing the swap-back corrupts the array for sibling iterations. For [1,2,3] at start=0, after processing j=1 (swap gives [2,1,3]) without swapping back, the j=2 iteration starts from [2,1,3] instead of [1,2,3] — producing wrong permutations silently.

items: Adding the array directly to results rather than copying it means all entries share the same array reference — they all end up showing the final state.
Forgetting the swap-back corrupts state for all sibling branches without throwing any error.

speakable_v2.cap: Swap before recursing, swap back after — without both halves the state is permanently corrupted.

questions.title: Backtracking vs Dynamic Programming: How to Decide
questions.direct_answer: Use **backtracking** when you must **enumerate or construct all valid solutions** (permutations, subsets, N-Queens, Sudoku) - it explores the whole decision tree with pruning. Use **dynamic programming** when you need an **optimal value or a count** and the problem has **overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure** (knapsack, LCS, coin change). interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can route a problem to backtracking (enumerate all) vs DP (optimize/count with overlap)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using backtracking where DP's memoization is needed (exponential blowup), or vice versa
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Key signal: 'list all solutions' -> backtracking; 'best/number of ways' + overlapping subproblems -> DP

sections.title: Backtracking vs Dynamic Programming
sections.content:
Both explore a space of choices, but they answer different questions. **Backtracking** is for **enumeration and construction**: 'find **all** valid arrangements/solutions' - permutations, subsets, combinations, N-Queens, Sudoku, word search. It walks the **decision tree**, pruning dead branches, and is frequently **exponential** because the answer set itself can be huge.

**Dynamic programming** is for **optimization or counting** when the problem has **overlapping subproblems** (the same subproblem recurs) and **optimal substructure** (an optimal solution is built from optimal sub-solutions) - knapsack, longest common subsequence, coin change, edit distance. DP **memoizes** or tabulates subproblem results so each is solved **once**, turning exponential recursion into **polynomial** time. Rule of thumb: 'list/construct all' -> backtracking; 'best value or how many ways' with reuse -> DP.

sections.content:
| Aspect | Backtracking | Dynamic Programming |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | Enumerate/construct all solutions | Optimal value or count |
| Needs | Validity check + pruning | Overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure |
| Reuses subproblems? | No | Yes (memo/table) |
| Typical time | Exponential | Polynomial |
| Examples | Permutations, subsets, N-Queens | Knapsack, LCS, coin change |

sections.title: Backtracking - enumerate all subsets
DP - count ways (reuse subproblems)
When to Use Each
sections.content:
- **Backtracking**: the task is to **list or build every valid solution**, or to find *a* solution to a constraint puzzle (Sudoku, N-Queens). Pruning is your main optimization.
- **DP**: the task asks for the **optimum** (min/max) or a **count of ways**, and the same subproblems repeat - memoize (top-down) or tabulate (bottom-up).
- **Hybrid**: some problems start as backtracking and become DP once you add memoization on repeated states.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Backtracking**: enumerate/construct **all** solutions; often **exponential**.
- **DP**: **optimize or count** with **overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure**.
- DP **reuses** subproblem answers (memo/table) -> **polynomial**.
- Signal: 'list all' -> backtracking; 'best / how many ways' -> DP.
- Memoizing a backtracking recursion can turn it into DP.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The way I decide is by looking at what the problem is actually asking for. Backtracking is for enumeration and construction, when I need to find all valid solutions or build a solution to a constraint problem. Classic examples are generating all permutations, all subsets, all combinations, or solving N-Queens and Sudoku. Backtracking walks the entire decision tree, choosing, exploring, and undoing, with pruning to skip dead branches, and it's frequently exponential, partly because the set of answers itself can be exponential. Dynamic programming, on the other hand, is for optimization or counting, when I need the best value, like a minimum or maximum, or the number of ways to do something. DP applies when the problem has two properties: overlapping subproblems, meaning the same smaller problem comes up again and again, and optimal substructure, meaning an optimal solution is composed of optimal solutions to subproblems. Examples are knapsack, longest common subsequence, coin change, and edit distance. The whole point of DP is that it solves each subproblem once and reuses the answer, through memoization top-down or tabulation bottom-up, which collapses what would be exponential recursion into polynomial time. So my quick test is: if the problem says list all or construct every solution, I reach for backtracking; if it says find the best or count the number of ways, and I notice repeated subproblems, I reach for DP. And there's a nice connection between them: many problems start as a backtracking recursion that's too slow, and the moment I add memoization over the repeated states, it effectively becomes dynamic programming.

speakable_v2.hook: Ask one question of the problem - 'list them all' or 'give me the best one?' - and it tells you backtracking or DP.

groups.heading: Backtracking
groups.text: Explores all valid paths through a search space and collects every complete solution. The state is the current path — unique per branch — so it can't be cached. Used when the problem says 'list all', 'enumerate', or 'generate all'. Examples: all permutations, all subsets, N-Queens, word search.

groups.heading: Dynamic programming
groups.text: Breaks a problem into overlapping subproblems, caches each result, and builds up to the final answer. The state is a cacheable scalar or vector — the same subproblem appears across many branches. Used when the problem says 'minimum', 'maximum', 'how many ways', or 'is it possible'. Examples: coin change, LCS, 0/1 knapsack.

items: Pick backtracking when the problem uses the words 'find all', 'list all', or 'generate all' — the full path matters and can't be summarised.
Pick DP when the problem uses 'minimum', 'maximum', 'number of ways', or 'is it possible' and the same sub-amount or sub-index is visited from many branches.

beats.text: non-obvious: Counting the number of paths in a grid is DP — only the count matters per cell, not which specific path. Listing all paths is backtracking — two paths that reach the same cell via different routes are both valid and must both be recorded.

speakable_v2.cap: Ask yourself: does order or the specific path matter in the answer? If yes, backtrack. If only the scalar result matters, reach for DP.
